title: Bangladesh Just Tied the Future of India Relations to a 30-Year-Old Water Treaty. The Clock Runs Out in December.
excerpt: Dhaka's ruling BNP has made renewal of the 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty a precondition for bilateral ties — and is building its own barrage on the Padma as a fallback. For millions on both sides of the border, the stakes are existential.
body:
Bangladesh's ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party has publicly declared that the future of Dhaka's relationship with New Delhi hinges on the successful renewal of the Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, the 30-year-old agreement that expires in December 2026. In a statement that diplomatic observers have characterised as unusually blunt, BNP minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir said the country's ties with India "will depend on renewing the Ganges water-sharing treaty to meet the needs of Bangladesh's people."

## A Treaty Under Strain

The 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty regulates the distribution of the Ganges flow at the Farakka Barrage in West Bengal — India's massive dam across the river, built in the 1970s to flush silt from the Hooghly River and keep Calcutta's port navigable. Under the agreement, India and Bangladesh share the dry-season flow according to a formula based on measured discharge levels, with Bangladesh guaranteed a minimum allocation when flows fall below 70,000 cusecs.

But Dhaka has complained for years that the actual water released during the lean season is consistently less than what the treaty promises. Bangladesh's position is that India's upstream withdrawals — for irrigation, industry, and river-linking projects — have reduced the Ganges flow to levels that threaten agriculture, drinking water supply, and the ecology of the Sundarbans delta, the world's largest mangrove forest and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The BNP government, which came to power after the political upheaval that ended Sheikh Hasina's Awami League government, has taken a markedly harder line on water issues than its predecessor. Party leaders have ordered the government to begin "immediate talks" with New Delhi on a fresh pact that reflects Bangladesh's expectations, and Bangladesh has approved a major Padma barrage project — its own dam on the river, which is called the Padma once it crosses the border — as a hedge against continued Indian control of upstream flows.

## The Numbers at Stake

Bangladesh is seeking a guaranteed allocation of 40,000 cusecs during the dry season, a significant increase from what the current formula typically delivers. India has reportedly signalled openness to renewal but prefers a shorter-term agreement, while Bangladesh wants a longer pact that provides greater certainty. A joint technical committee is being formed to review hydrological data and propose revised terms.

The water dispute extends beyond the Ganges. The Teesta River agreement, which was nearly signed under the previous Bangladeshi government but collapsed due to opposition from West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee, remains unresolved. Bangladesh has also raised concerns about India's broader river-linking programme, which could divert water from shared rivers.

## Why This Matters to the Diaspora

The Ganges water dispute touches the Indian and Bangladeshi diasporas in ways that extend beyond geopolitics. For the millions of Bangladeshi-origin immigrants in the United States, United Kingdom, and the Gulf states, the health of the Ganges-Padma system is directly tied to the livelihoods of families back home. Agriculture in southwestern Bangladesh — the region most dependent on the Ganges flow — supports some of the poorest communities in the country, and water scarcity during the dry season has been a driver of rural-to-urban migration and, ultimately, emigration.

For Indian-origin communities, particularly those with roots in West Bengal, the Farakka Barrage is a source of both pride and controversy. The dam saved Calcutta's port but fundamentally altered the hydrology of the lower Ganges, contributing to riverbank erosion, groundwater depletion, and the ecological degradation of the Sundarbans on both sides of the border.

The approaching deadline has also drawn attention from environmental and climate advocacy groups in the diaspora, who argue that any renewed treaty must account for climate change — shrinking Himalayan glaciers, shifting monsoon patterns, and rising sea levels in the Bay of Bengal — factors that were not part of the 1996 agreement.

## The Countdown

With seven months until the treaty expires, the diplomatic calendar is tight. India-Bangladesh relations have been fraught since the BNP's return to power, with disputes over border management, minority rights, and trade creating a difficult backdrop for water negotiations. Dhaka's decision to frame the treaty renewal as a precondition for broader bilateral ties raises the pressure on New Delhi but also narrows the room for compromise.

If the treaty lapses without renewal, there is no legal framework governing how the Ganges is shared during the dry season — a scenario that would leave Bangladesh exposed to India's unilateral decisions and potentially trigger a humanitarian and ecological crisis in one of the world's most densely populated regions.
